title: Zeno's shipwreck
hookLine: a merchant loses his cargo of purple dye off Athens and wanders into a bookshop
carry: I sailed well when I was wrecked

lines: THE MAN WHO STARTED IT ALL.
cards: A merchant ship, carrying a cargo of purple dye from Phoenicia, goes down somewhere off the coast near Athens. The cargo, the fortune, gone into the sea. The merchant makes it to shore with, as far as we know, nothing.
His name is Zeno, from Citium, a city on the island of Cyprus. Centuries before the emperor and the enslaved teacher, he's the man who started it all.

teach.b: Our source is Diogenes Laërtius, who wrote lives of the Greek philosophers centuries after Zeno, collecting stories from older books, some already disagreeing.
So this is the story the ancient world told about Zeno, not a court record.
Shipwrecked, broke, around thirty years old, Zeno walks up from the harbor into Athens. He doesn't know anyone. He wanders into a bookseller's shop and sits down.
The bookseller is reading aloud, or Zeno picks up, a book about Socrates, written by one of Socrates's students. Zeno is hooked.

The way Socrates lived, questioning everything, owning almost nothing, unafraid, hits him right in the chest. He's lost everything he owned, and on the same trip he finds what he'll spend the rest of his life on.
Years later, Diogenes says, Zeno looked back on the wreck and said something like: I made a good voyage when I was shipwrecked. Another version has him thanking Fortune for driving him to philosophy.

Either way, the man who lost a fortune at sea founded a school that would reach an emperor in his tent, an enslaved teacher in Nicopolis, and people reading the Stoics on their phones today. Now, gently.

teach.h: NOT EVERY LOSS IS A GIFT.
teach.b: Not every loss sends you somewhere good, and nobody should tell a grieving person that everything happens for a reason.

teach.h: I SAILED WELL WHEN I WAS WRECKED.
teach.b: The Stoics didn't say the wreck was good. They said what you do after the wreck is still yours. Zeno's cargo sank.

how: Stoics practice looking at a setback as material to work with rather than simply a disaster, asking what response is still in their power after the loss.

o: a Greek myth about a hero lost on his long way home
the shipwreck that set the Stoic school in motion
a Stoic exercise of imagining you've lost everything

games.q: you're Zeno. your ship has sunk with everything you own, and you've washed up near Athens knowing no one. where do you end up?
o: in a bookshop, reading about Socrates.
games.why: he wanders into a bookseller's shop and finds a book about Socrates. he later said he made a good voyage when he was shipwrecked.

practice: Sit, and let the breath settle, then look back for one loss that, in the end, sent you somewhere good: a job that ended, a plan that fell through, a move you didn't want.
Not the worst loss, just one where you can see the bookshop now: what sank, and where you washed up. If none comes, that's all right; rest in the breath.
